population.note: FICTIONAL. Of ~275M adults: 30.4% current ≈ 83.6M; 41.5% ever ≈ 114.1M; used-and-off-now 11.1% ≈ 30.5M; never-used ≈ 161M. Cycling arithmetic: ever 41.5 − current 30.4 = 11.1 pts off now; ≈14.0 pts of current users are on a second or later course and ≈4.5 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once and stopped again, so (14.0+4.5)/41.5 ≈ 45% cycled. That is consistent with the starting world's ~35% one-year persistence and 36–47% restart within a year. Ever-use rose 6.0 pts (limit 8.4) and current rose 5.4. Most growth came from people restarting: commercial users dropped by employers after the 2033 price rise moved to $149–229 cash orals or to imports instead of stopping. Age check: 18–29 17% × 52M = 8.8M; 30–49 33% × 91M = 30.0M; 50–64 44% × 62M = 27.3M; 65+ 25% × 70M = 17.5M; total ≈ 83.6M = 30.4%. The 65+ band rose from 17% to 25% because Part D obesity eligibility widened in Jan 2034 to BMI ≥27 without a comorbidity (≈1.6M added) and because cash 'metabolic' regimens spread among non-obese retirees (≈1.5M of the 65+ users are not paid by Medicare). Roughly one in five 65+ ever-users is still off on a medically advised bone pause. Income: the bottom third rose 21→28%, mostly through Medicaid re-enrolment after 2032's six-month suspensions expired and through ≈7.6M users of imported or counterfeit product (under-measured and concentrated in the bottom third). The top third rose 28→33% through 'metabolic' and longevity use among people without obesity. Of the ~30.5M off-now: ≈6M are on bone or DEXA pauses, ≈9M lost coverage or were suspended under gating, ≈11M stopped for GI effects, anhedonia or cost, and ≈4.5M are pregnant, trying to conceive, or stopped by contraindication. The ~161M never-users are disproportionately under-30, rural residents of non-expansion states, people with contraindications, and refusers by conviction. Pediatric: 1.1% of ~73M under-18s ≈ 800k, mostly adolescents 12+. Off-label oral use in 10–14-year-olds is growing and is the least measured part of the figure. About two children in five now live with a parent who is on the drug or cycling off it.

access.public_coverage: FICTIONAL. Medicare Part D obesity benefit: the $199 negotiated rate and $50 copay are unchanged, because the rate is contracted through Dec 2035. The Jan 2034 appropriations package extended eligibility to BMI ≥27 without a comorbidity and added the Wegovy pill 50 mg at the same rate. Medicare pays 20.8% of fills ≈ 17.4M users (16.0M aged 65+ plus ≈1.4M disabled under-65): ≈6.3M diabetes and ≈11.1M obesity. Obesity-benefit gross 11.1M × $199 × 12 ≈ $26.5B, less beneficiary copays 11.1M × $50 × 12 ≈ $6.7B, leaves ≈$19.8B to the program. All Medicare incretin fills: 17.4M × $199 × 12 ≈ $41.6B gross. CBO score of the 2034 widening: ≈1.6M added users × ($199 − $50) × 12 ≈ $2.9B/yr, or ≈$29B over 2034–43. Like the 2031 score, it excludes Part A fracture and fall costs. Medicaid: the 90% federal match for continuation-standard states is unchanged. Coverage now runs in 35 states plus DC, because four states (Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Nevada, Virginia) had enacted adoption laws in 2032 that took effect in Jan 2033. Medicaid pays 16.3% of fills ≈ 13.6M × $199 × 12 ≈ $32.5B gross before supplemental rebates. Public programmes combined pay 37.1% of fills, more than commercial plans (31.1%), so the public payer is now the default.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 100+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month, oral semaglutide generics at $8–25, and tirzepatide copies, legal under India's patent position, at $25–40. China: domestic semaglutide and tirzepatide generics, and its API underlies almost all of the US gray trade. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 50–80. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and Egypt have generics, and Mexico's border pharmacies are a major US source. US: the 2031 settlement allowed generic semaglutide entry in 2033, but the first-to-file holder's Hyderabad plant has been under an FDA import alert since Apr 2033. Its parked 180-day exclusivity blocks the other settled filers. An FTC forfeiture suit is pending, and entry is now expected in 2035.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Shock up. Three things combined in 2033: the generic semaglutide launch slipped, a sterility-related pen recall and shortage listing hit Lilly's contract fill-finish network (Jun 2033 to Jan 2034), and Section 232 tariffs stayed in place. In Jul 2033 Novo and Lilly raised direct-portal injectable prices from $199–279 to $249–349. Retatrutide went from $399 to $449 direct and from $1,499 to $1,599 list, amycretin to $499 direct, and survodutide launched at $429. Oral starting doses stayed at $149. High-dose orals (Wegovy pill 50 mg, Foundayo top dose) cost $199–229. PBM commercial net rose from ≈$170–190 to ≈$215–240. Employer coverage fell from 66% to 61%, mainly among small and mid-size firms, and ≈80% of covering plans are gated. Payer mix of ≈83.6M users: commercial 31.1% (26.0M), Medicare 20.8% (17.4M), Medicaid 16.3% (13.6M), cash/direct 22.7% (19.0M, including ≈4.0M 'calm/focus' and ≈4.0M 'metabolic/longevity' subscribers without obesity), imported/counterfeit 9.1% (7.6M). Sum 83.6M = 100%. Orals are ≈53% of fills, up from ≈38% in 2032, because of the injectable shortage, the 50 mg parity label and the price gap. Imports doubled from 3.8M. The 503B exclusion and 503A injunction stand.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, incl. 7.2 mg)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, incl. 12 mg maintenance)
GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, approved Mar 2033)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill incl. 50 mg maintenance from Sep 2033, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 small-molecule, daily oral (orforglipron: Foundayo, incl. maintenance-after-injectable label)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' and longevity regimens in people with BMI 22–29 and no diabetes (≈4.0M on low-dose oral semaglutide or Foundayo). They moved from concierge practices into telehealth chains and employer lifestyle catalogues.
'calm' and 'focus' subscriptions (≈4.0M, flat since the anhedonia label)
scheduled 'drug holidays' (weekend or event skips of daily orals) to manage reward blunting
smoking and vaping cessation (trial read out 2034, no filing yet)
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care, plus unsupervised family sharing of oral packs
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. The oral_parity driver is realised by an existing product in a new form. In Sep 2033 FDA approved a 50 mg maintenance dose of the Wegovy pill on a 72-week head-to-head trial: 16.8% mean loss versus 16.1% for injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg, which met noninferiority. At the same time Foundayo gained a label for maintenance after switching from injectable induction. The parity is with injectable semaglutide. No pill matches tirzepatide or retatrutide 12 mg, but for the median user the needle is no longer necessary. Oral amycretin is in phase 3 and not on the market. Survodutide was approved Mar 2033 for chronic weight management (≈19% loss, heart-rate precaution, DEXA monitoring). MariTide received a complete response letter in Jul 2033 asking for more bone data, was resubmitted in Apr 2034, and has a decision due in 2035. Lilly filed bimagrumab + tirzepatide in Jun 2034, the first lean-mass-sparing filing, with a decision no earlier than mid-2035. The smoking-cessation trial (2034) met its abstinence endpoint but showed worse SHAPS scores in the active arm, and no filing has been made. No new approved indication this step. Incretin market ≈$213B in 2034. US ≈$188B: public 31.0M × $199 ≈ $6.17B/month, commercial 26.0M × ~$225 ≈ $5.85B, cash 19.0M × ~$190 ≈ $3.61B, for ≈$15.6B/month × 12. Ex-US ≈$25B and eroding under generics.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect. Restart nausea after drug holidays is now a large share of complaints. GI rates at 50 mg oral are comparable to injectable.
Rising in absolute numbers with more users aged 65+ and on high-dose triple agonists.
No causal confirmation. Counterfeit and imported product confound reporting more than ever.
With 17.5M users aged 65+, the 2034 Medicare claims update estimates ≈1.9M long-term older users meet sarcopenia criteria. Lean mass is still ~30–40% of weight lost in untrained users over 50.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label retained. Body-composition monitoring is in the retatrutide 12 mg, amycretin and survodutide labels. The CMS annual DEXA rule for long-term 65+ users is unchanged.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ≈8.0M users aged 65+ have more than 2 years' use. At a ~0.6%/yr baseline hip-fracture rate × 0.35 excess, that is ≈16,800 excess hip fractures a year, plus vertebral fractures in cycling postmenopausal women. DEXA waits have eased to 8–14 weeks as mobile capacity grew, but remain longest in the rural South.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelling retained; bone endpoints required in new filings (cited in the MariTide CRL); the CMS 90-day bone-pause code is unchanged; the DOJ civil case against Novo is unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; no class determination.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association, and the 2033 anhedonia review explicitly separated it from reward blunting.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Labelled Nov 2033 with a prevalence estimate. In the pooled analysis, clinically meaningful anhedonia (SHAPS threshold) was reported in 11.8% of retatrutide 12 mg users versus 5.1% of comparators, 6–7% versus 4–5% at top tirzepatide and semaglutide doses, and showed no detectable excess at low oral doses (studies underpowered). If causal, ≈8M top-dose users × ~7 pts ≈ 560k excess cases, plus ≈45M standard-dose users × ~1.5 pts ≈ 680k, for ≈1.2M excess cases. It usually resolves within 2–6 weeks of dose reduction.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA safety labeling change under 505(o)(4) for the class: Warnings and Precautions for high-dose triple and dual agonists, Adverse Reactions for all, and a SHAPS-based screening recommendation. The FTC consent orders stand. No REMS.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Larger again because of the 2033 shortage-forced stops, employer coverage drops and continued gating.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The CMS bone-pause code applies to Medicare and Medicaid. Private plans still have no equivalent. The Seventh Circuit has not ruled on the Indiana waiver.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D, calcium and protein insufficiency are common in high-loss older users. Non-obese 'metabolic' users on low doses show protein insufficiency in small studies.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance; Part D counselling screen continues; no FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~10 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About twelve years of follow-up. The adolescent bone-accrual signal is unresolved, and the full dataset is due 2034–35 and partly delayed. Off-label oral use in 10–14-year-olds is unstudied.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements continue; FDA reiterated the 2034 adolescent data deadline, and sponsors asked for an extension.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The worst year since 2029. Imports doubled to ≈7.6M users. In 2034 the CDC reported a cluster of counterfeit 'Zepbound' pens filled with insulin across Texas, Arizona and Florida: 214 hospitalisations for severe hypoglycaemia and 7 deaths. Separately there were ~160 nontuberculous mycobacterial injection-site infections from unlabelled vials, and assays of imported oral tablets found 40–160% of stated content. Poison-centre incretin calls rose ~45% on 2032.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts, the largest coordinated mail-facility seizure operation to date, and a CDC health advisory. The 'Safe Pens' authentication bill passed the House and stalled in the Senate. Individuals are still not prosecuted.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent, higher at 12 mg; usually transient.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Persistently higher fall-related ED visits in long-term 65+ users. Absolute numbers are rising with the larger Medicare population.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening is mandatory in the Part D counselling visit.

safety_ledger.effect: Adverse body-composition cycling (fat-dominant regain after lean-dominant loss)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: DEXA cohorts confirm the pattern and add the 2033 shortage-forced stops as a natural experiment. The effect is concentrated in bottom-third users cycled by coverage loss.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Joint society guidance recommends resistance training and protein during any pause; no regulatory action.

safety_ledger.effect: Heart-rate elevation at high triple-agonist and glucagon-containing doses
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen with retatrutide 12 mg and survodutide; arrhythmia significance unclear.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled as a precaution on both; cardiovascular outcomes trials ongoing.

safety_ledger.effect: Restart toxicity after unsupervised drug holidays (severe vomiting, dehydration, acute kidney injury)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New entry. ED reports of severe GI events in users who resume a full maintenance dose after 1–3 weeks off without re-titrating. Older users on diuretics are at higher risk. Rate unknown.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA drug safety communication on re-titration (2034); pharmacist counselling guidance. Over-the-counter 'restart' packs remain unregulated.

food_and_beverage.state: With three adults in ten on the drug, US salty-snack volume is falling ~4% a year and confectionery ~5–6%. A third large food group sold its candy unit in 2033. Demand is splitting by income: premium 'lean-mass' protein and bone-fortified dairy lead at Whole Foods-tier grocers, while dollar-channel calorie-dense value packs hold volume in bottom-third neighbourhoods where users cycle off. 'On-plan' aisles are standard.

alcohol.state: Seventh straight year of US spirits volume decline, with beer down too. The anhedonia label produced a small premium-wine 'holiday weekend' bump. Some users time drug holidays around weddings and drink more on those days, which distributors call 'event drinking'.

restaurants.state: Spend per cover is down ~10–12% from 2028 in high-uptake suburbs. Gram-priced bowls are the default. Fine-dining 'holiday tasting menus' sell to users skipping a weekend dose. Value buffets keep closing. Heritage 'full table' rooms in Atlanta, Memphis and Houston are still busy.

apparel.state: Sizing is stratifying. Upscale brands cut for trained shoulders and narrow waists ('the coached cut'). Mid-market brands carry wide size runs for cycling customers. Resale and rental sized for cycling keep growing.

fitness.state: Growing. 'Prescribed lifting' is standard in Medicare Advantage, and DEXA-plus-coaching chains are in most metro strip malls. Premium 'lean index' gyms in Scottsdale, Buckhead and Austin charge $300+/month and post members' DEXA percentiles. Coaching for older lifters is still short of staff.

insurance.state: Contracting. The 2033 price rise drove pharmacy trend to ~+14%, and employer coverage fell from 66% to 61%, mostly at firms under 500 employees. Surviving plans tightened gating (≈80%) and capped cumulative months. Employers push retirees and over-65 workers onto Part D. Life insurers still ask untreated BMI ≥30 applicants why they are not on treatment.

pharma.state: Growing on price and volume. Lilly leads through tirzepatide, retatrutide and Foundayo despite the 2033 pen recall. Novo regained share with the 50 mg pill and Medicare semaglutide. Boehringer entered with survodutide. Indian generic makers are locked out of the US by the import alert and the parked exclusivity, and supply the gray market instead.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Income, more than whether someone is treated. Being on the drug is unremarkable. The visible question is which regimen and how well it is supervised. Trained shoulders, a flat waist and a good 'lean index' signal coached retatrutide or amycretin with DEXA on schedule. 'Kiosk soft' — a regain shape of fuller midsection and thin arms after a coverage loss or a Medicaid suspension — signals the continuation standard. Very lean, slack-armed bodies with no muscle tone read as cheap imported pens.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Use levels have nearly converged (bottom 28% against top 33%), but body composition now tracks income. In Phoenix, the Scottsdale lean-index gyms and the Maryvale pharmacy kiosks are fifteen miles apart and produce recognisably different bodies. Columbus has the same split between Upper Arlington and the Hilltop. Among non-obese top-third professionals, 'metabolic' low-dose regimens are a form of upkeep, like teeth whitening. Hiring managers deny that they read bodies, and a 2034 Pew survey finds 41% of adults believe others do.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Protein-first shared meals are the default. Drug-holiday dinners are a new form: friends coordinate a skipped weekend so everyone is hungry together, and hosts ask 'are we off Saturday?' Church potlucks and full-table rooms persist as heritage.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: The apps' on/off/pausing field now includes 'holiday weekends'. Daters infer income from regimen ('retatrutide plus coach' versus 'Medicaid oral'), and some profiles list a DEXA percentile. Advice columns field complaints about partners who are 'grey' on top doses.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Managed, and increasingly scheduled. Appetite is something you switch back on for occasions. The backlash coalition persists and has gained disability lawyers' arguments about the PDC rule penalising holidays. Atlanta's body-sovereignty collectives have begun to frame the class-coded body as a new redlining.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Labelled Nov 2033: 11.8% versus 5.1% at retatrutide 12 mg, 6–7% versus 4–5% at top tirzepatide and semaglutide doses, and no measurable excess at low oral doses. That implies ≈1.2M excess cases if causal (≈560k among ≈8M top-dose users plus ≈680k among ≈45M standard-dose users). A 2034 KFF poll finds 38% of current users report 'feeling flat' at some point, 22% have taken a deliberate drug holiday in the past year, and 14% have stepped down a dose for mood rather than for GI effects.
interior_life.framing: Side effect, openly named. 'The grey' is now a label term in the patient insert ('loss of interest or pleasure'). Telehealth brands rebranded from 'calm' to 'metabolic', selling the same pill and dose under a different story. Clinicians talk about 'titrating for affect'. A drug holiday is treated as self-care, not non-compliance, except by the plans that count missed days.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Employers' lifestyle catalogues moved 'focus' subscriptions under 'metabolic health' after the label. Sales, hospitality and creative workers schedule doses around peaks. Unions now fight over the gating rule (≥80% PDC), which counts weekend holidays as non-adherence: two days off a week leaves about 71%. Some 2034 contracts code a 'holiday allowance'. Fleets and warehouses still favour continuous dosing.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Grey era' has become a standard critical term. 'Holiday shows' — late-Saturday comedy and live-music bills marketed to people off for the weekend — are a Nashville and Austin staple. Extreme sports and very spicy food keep growing. Some novelists publicise writing on a dose step-down.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples schedule holidays together, and pharmacies stock 'restart' anti-nausea packs beside condoms. Sex therapists use SHAPS at intake. 'Are you grey right now?' is a common question between partners.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Prices and counterfeits dominate. The insulin-pen deaths and the July 2033 price rise made 'why is the pill cheaper in Toronto' a midterm ad line in both parties. Disability advocates, unions and backlash groups have converged on the PDC rule's treatment of drug holidays. No party proposes ending public coverage.

state.regulatory_posture: FDA is data-demanding and now openly labels harms. It ran the class anhedonia labeling change, issued the MariTide CRL on bone data, approved oral 50 mg parity and survodutide, and issued a re-titration safety communication. Import enforcement escalated through a coordinated seizure operation, but there are still no individual prosecutions and no importation law. The FTC is suing over the parked generic exclusivity.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Public expansion, mostly built on earlier law. The Jan 2034 appropriations package widened Part D obesity eligibility to BMI ≥27 and added the 50 mg pill at $199/$50. Medicaid enhanced match now runs in 35 states plus DC through 2032-enacted laws. No individual mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: No new state action this step. The CMS continuation standard (Dec 2031) is unchanged: ≥80% PDC, a verified weight every 6 months, a 5% response threshold at 6 months or clinician override, annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users, the 90-day bone-pause code, and a 6-month suspension after two misses. The Indiana and Arkansas 12-month rules continue. Private gating covers ≈80% of employer plans. BMI-linked wellness surcharges continue.
state.workforce_or_military: Unchanged in rule. DOT sleep-apnea screening still pushes drivers toward tirzepatide, and the 2033 pen shortage forced fleets to switch drivers to orals. The Army accession debate is still contested; the Air Force waiver policy is unchanged.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: India and China supply the world's generics and the US gray market. The FDA import alert on the first-filer's Hyderabad plant became a US–India trade irritant, and the 2032 'pharmaceutical parcel cooperation' clause produced joint seizure work but no legal channel. Section 232 tariffs remain. Lilly's 2033 contract fill-finish recall exposed how concentrated pen capacity is, and the shift to pills — tablet capacity is easier to build — is partly a supply-chain response.

events.event: FDA places the Hyderabad plant of the first-to-file semaglutide generic maker on import alert after sterility failures. Its parked 180-day exclusivity freezes every other settled filer, and the 2033 generic launch slips. In July Novo and Lilly raise direct-portal injectable prices to $249–349, citing tariffs and a pen-line recall.

FDA approves a 50 mg maintenance dose of the Wegovy pill after a head-to-head trial shows 16.8% weight loss against 16.1% for injectable semaglutide. Foundayo gains a label for switching from injectables. Within a year more than half of US incretin fills are pills.

FDA orders a class-wide labeling change naming anhedonia and emotional blunting as an adverse reaction, with prevalence of 11.8% versus 5.1% at top-dose retatrutide, and recommends routine screening. Telehealth brands rename 'calm' plans 'metabolic' within weeks.

The January appropriations package widens Medicare's obesity benefit to anyone with a BMI of 27 or more and adds the 50 mg pill at the $199 rate. CBO scores it at about $29 billion over ten years, excluding fracture costs. Public programmes now pay for more incretin fills than employers do.

CDC reports 214 hospitalisations and 7 deaths from counterfeit 'Zepbound' pens filled with insulin across Texas, Arizona and Florida, as imported and counterfeit users reach an estimated 7.6 million. A House-passed pen-authentication bill stalls in the Senate.

A JAMA cohort linking low-dose oral use in adults with BMI 22–27 to lower all-cause mortality drives 'metabolic' subscriptions past 4 million, despite healthy-user-bias warnings. The same month a Pew survey finds 41% of adults believe employers judge income and discipline from body shape.

open_tensions: Generic semaglutide is stuck behind a parked exclusivity at a plant under import alert, while Medicare's $199 rate is contracted through Dec 2035. When generics arrive, public programmes paying for 31M users will be paying several times the world price, and 7.6M Americans already pay that world price through the mail.

The continuation standard's ≥80% PDC rule counts the drug holidays that the new anhedonia label effectively endorses as non-adherence. A user taking weekends off scores about 71% and risks suspension. Unions, disability lawyers and clinicians all want a 'holiday code', and CMS has not acted.

Medicare is now paying for 17.4M users while ≈16,800 excess hip fractures a year and ≈1.9M sarcopenic seniors are billed to Part A and Medicare Advantage, outside every CBO score. The 2034 widening added more long-horizon older users.

Body composition now tracks income. Coached, scanned, lean-mass-protected regimens are bought privately, while the public and gray-market tiers produce cycling, fat-dominant regain. Nothing in the coverage law addresses the difference, and employers deny that they read it.
still_true: The CMS continuation standard's terms are unchanged from the Dec 2031 final rule: ≥80% PDC, a verified six-monthly weigh-in, a 5% response threshold, annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users, and the 90-day 'bone pause' code.
The Medicare Part D obesity rate is still $199 a month with a $50 beneficiary copay, and the counselling visit is kept.
Oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) are still $149 a month cash through the federal direct-pricing portal (launched as TrumpRx) and manufacturer direct channels.
The 503B exclusion and the 503A injunction against compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide still stand, and individuals using imported pens are still not prosecuted.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.

prose.headline: The Pill Caught Up With the Pen, the Price Went Up Anyway, and Now Your Shoulders Show Your Pay
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 three American adults in ten are on an incretin drug, and most of them take it as a pill. Few people say so directly, but you can see on someone's body whether they can pay for good care.

The pill arrived first. In September 2033 the FDA approved a 50-milligram Wegovy tablet that matched the injectable in a head-to-head trial. It did not match the triple agonist, and the strongest results still need a pen. But for the typical patient the needle was no longer necessary. The timing mattered, because the pens had become scarce and expensive. In April 2033 the FDA put the Indian plant that held first rights to generic semaglutide on import alert, and the other generic makers were legally barred from launching ahead of it. The generic everyone had planned around for 2033 did not come. A sterility recall then emptied part of Lilly's pen supply, and in July both manufacturers raised portal prices on injectables to between $249 and $349. Starter pills stayed at $149. Employers' pharmacy costs rose sharply, and one in thirteen covering employers, most of them small firms, dropped the drug.

The public programmes picked those patients up. Medicare's rate is still $199, fixed by contract through 2035. In January Congress opened the benefit to anyone with a BMI of 27 or more. Medicaid's enhanced match now runs in thirty-five states and Washington, D.C. Public programmes now pay for more fills than employers do, which no one planned and few people have noticed. The continuation standard is exactly as CMS wrote it in 2031: the pharmacy kiosk weigh-in, the five-percent threshold, the annual bone scan for long-term seniors, and the ninety-day bone pause.

The people who could not wait for 2035 buy from the mail. About 7.6 million Americans inject or swallow drugs from Hyderabad, Shenzhen or Tijuana, double the 2032 figure. In May the CDC traced counterfeit Zepbound pens filled with insulin through Texas, Arizona and Florida. Two hundred people were hospitalised for blood sugar crashes and seven died. The House passed a pen-authentication bill and the Senate let it sit.

The grey now has a label. In November 2033 the FDA added emotional blunting to every incretin's prescribing information: about twelve percent of top-dose triple-agonist users against five percent of comparators, smaller excesses at standard doses, and nothing detectable at low oral doses. It became an ordinary complaint, the way insomnia is for some antidepressants. People step down a dose before a wedding. Friends coordinate a weekend off so they will all be hungry at the same dinner. Pharmacies sell restart nausea packs at the counter, and emergency rooms see people who went straight back to a full dose. The gated plans count every skipped day against the eighty-percent adherence rule, and so do the public programmes. Unions and disability lawyers now make the same argument.

The same low-dose pill that was sold as 'calm' is now sold as 'metabolic.' Four million people without obesity take it as upkeep, because an observational study suggested they would live longer and because their benefits catalogue lists it beside the meditation app.

The result is that bodies now show which tier of care someone is in. In Scottsdale, gyms post members' lean-mass percentiles next to the squat racks. Fifteen miles west, in Maryvale, the kiosk by the blood-pressure cuff records the weight of people who lost coverage for six months and regained it mostly as belly fat. Coached retatrutide gives you shoulders, and cycling on Medicaid gives you a soft middle and thin arms. Cheap imported pens leave people gaunt and slack. Hiring managers say they do not notice the difference. Forty-one percent of Americans think they do.

The hip fractures are still billed to Part A, where no budget score looks.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Hollins sets the 50-milligram tablet on the counter at 6:10 and doesn't take it. It's Saturday. Kayla's recital is at two.

She works as a hygienist in Dayton. The practice dropped the drug in January, after the letter about 'pharmacy trend.' Now it's $229 a month on the portal, which nobody gets to count. Monday she'll take half a dose, Tuesday the full one, with ginger chews in her scrub pocket.

At nine she drives her mother to the DEXA van parked outside Grace Methodist. Arlene is seventy-seven, on a bone pause, and wants to know if the pause can be longer. The tech says that's a question for the doctor. In the van's waiting tent a man is passing around his phone with the CDC notice about the pens. 'My nephew gets his from Texas,' somebody says. Nobody answers.

At noon she eats a grilled-cheese sandwich and tastes it.

The recital is in the middle-school gym. Kayla is eleven and fierce in a sequined collar. At the pirouette Denise is crying, which surprises her, and then laughing at crying, which surprises her more. The mother beside her, from Oakwood, has shoulders like a swimmer. She says, 'Holiday?' Denise nods. 'Us too. Whole family. Honestly, the best day of the month.'

On the way out Kayla asks if she can have a burger, and Denise says yes to two.

That night she reads the insert she usually throws away: *loss of interest or pleasure.* She folds it into a square and puts it under the pill for Monday.
